I find that economists failed to find timeless determinants for deposit flows. Second, I explore how the conditions of the savings deposit market shaped the demand for macroeconomic forecast models, using the PFSF as a case study. I show that while the rising volatility led bank managers to seek sophisticated tools to predict deposit flows, the deregulation of the banking industry put the forecasting quality of macroeco-nomic models for individual banks to the test.

articles.title: ECONOMIC HISTORY AND DEVELOPMENT POLICY: DOUGLASS NORTH’S DISILLUSIONMENT WITH SIMPLISTIC, MARKET-ORIENTED POLICIES, 1950s–1990s
articles.abstract: This paper examines Douglass North’s evolving recommendations for economic development policy. Using archival material, it traces how North’s historical analysis of economic growth shaped his policy prescriptions from the start of his career through the 1990s. In the 1950s and 1960s, North attributed U.S. economic growth primarily to trade and productivity gains driven by the United States’ competitive market system and international trade, leading him to advocate market-oriented reforms. But from the 1970s onward, recognizing the critical role of institutions through his study of institutional history, he emphasized reducing transaction costs through extensive reforms in property rights and political systems. His archives reveal how his historical understanding of development made him increasingly skeptical of simplistic, market-oriented reforms and underscore the originality of his policy proposals for Latin America and Eastern Europe in the 1980s and 1990s.

articles.title: The Majority Report: AI Optimism and Public Support for Police Use of AI in Nine Countries
articles.authors: Philipp Lutscher, Antonia Schulde, Adrian Rauchfleisch, Andreas Jungherr

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Police forces increasingly use Artificial Intelligence in support of specific tasks, such as data analysis, identifying suspects and monitoring public spaces. These uses potentially expand the state’s coercive capacity. Yet we know little about how far people accept these tools across political contexts and how these views systematically relate to other attitudes. We ask whether support rests on views of the technology, the problem AI use addresses, or trust in the institution using it. We analyze a preregistered survey of 9,000 respondents in the United States, China, Taiwan, the United Kingdom, and five EU countries using Bayesian multilevel models. Support is high for most uses everywhere. It rests on general AI benefits, perceived crime trends, and trust in the police, which matters similarly across countries. In contrast, general AI risks, personal fear of crime, and trust in legal institutions play no substantive role on average. Acceptance thus primarily is connected with optimism about AI, a general but not personal sense of problem relevance, and trust in the police.

articles.title: From Albertus Magnus to Thomas Aquinas: The discursive foundations of the risk on merchants and trade
articles.abstract: Albert the Great set out the moral risk incurred by merchants using a varied lexicon that reflects the frequency of occurrences and the maximum loss. Thomas Aquinas, his disciple, summarised Albert’s text by adopting the lexicon of frequency, which, along with the lexicon of probability used on the subject of usury in his other early economic text, marks a new stage. Using Albert’s text as a starting point, Thomas also makes a number of changes that allow him to express the merchant’s risk as a professional risk, incurred through speech. The risk incurred by speech is not one of gossip, but of the justice of exchange through the information given and the price stated.

articles.title: Book Review of European and Chinese Histories of Economic Thought: Theories and Images of Good Governance by Iwo Amelung and Bertram Schefold (eds.)
articles.abstract: This collection of essays likely stems from two separate conferences held in Germany, with the editors aiming to create a grand comparison between European and Chinese economic thought. This ambitious goal mirrors the work of R. Bin Wong and Jean-Laurent Rosenthal, culminating in Before and Beyond Divergence: The Politics of Economic Change in China and Europe. Given Wong’s participation in the conference and the fact that his essay opens the volume, it’s reasonable to assume that he played a role in shaping the book's conceptual framework.

articles.title: 2025 HES Presidential Address: Frank H. Knight’s Last Lecture – Pivotal Ideas in the History of Economics
articles.abstract: Frank Knight’s work is examined through the lens provided by the posthumous publication of his essay “Economic History” in the Dictionary of the History of Ideas in 1973. Knight identified pivotal ideas in economics from Adam Smith’s Wealth of Nations until the time of his retirement from The University of Chicago, with some recognition of earlier contributions. The priority he gave to liberty within economics shows in the connection between Adam Smith and American independence. He then worked his way chronologically through a consideration of eight “moments” from classical economics, almost all declared errors. After identifying marginalism with the turn to economic science in three moments, he identified fifteen more moments that led to the development of a science focused on entrepreneurs and enterprises. Knight’s conclusion provides brief mention of six movements that claimed to conflict with economics, although Knight argued that none of them actually conflict.

articles.title: Book Review of The Truth of Liberal Economy: Jacques Rueff and John Maynard Keynes by Yasuo Gonjo, Kazuhiko Yago, and Patrick Fridenson
articles.abstract: Yasuo Gonjo’s The Truth of Liberal Economy, translated by Kazuhiko Yago, retraces the critical dialogue between Jacques Rueff and John Maynard Keynes from the interwar period through the major economic and monetary reforms of the twentieth century. At the same time, it sheds light on debates surrounding inflation, interest rates, unemployment insurance, monetary regimes, the role of central banks, the functioning of international institutions, adjustment mechanisms, as well as the controversies surrounding the construction of Europe and its subsequent transformations. These issues, far from belonging to the past, remain central to contemporary economic debates.

articles.title: In Defense of Monopoly: Merchant Guilds and the Emergence of Liberalism in Portugal
articles.authors: JHET Assistant, Miguel Dantas da Cruz
articles.abstract: Despite being questioned and criticised since classical antiquity, monopolistic institutions and practices have persisted for centuries. Indeed, they remain a contentious issue in modern-day political debates. Some have argued that the longevity of monopolistic institutions, such as guilds, was the result of political arrangements with public authorities. Others, however, claim that they persisted because they were useful and efficient institutions (for example, they were a means of knowledge transfer that ultimately helped Europe surpass Asia). Much less discussed is how such institutions defended themselves in the public arena against widespread criticism. Drawing upon underexplored source material held in the Portuguese National Archives (Arquivo Nacional da Torre do Tombo, ANTT), this article examines how Portuguese commercial guilds justified their monopolies and privileges in the early 1820s. The article shows that while the defense of monopolies did involve economic justifications, it nonetheless mostly emphasized the social impacts of commercial monopolies (positive externalities), in particular the formation of a reliable class of merchants and citizens.

articles.title: The Interdependence of Migration: How Relational Structures Organise Movement
articles.abstract: Migration theory emphasises that mobility decisions are embedded in relational structures, such as interpersonal networks and organisational pipelines, and therefore interdependent. Yet, the dominant empirical practice treats migration outcomes as determined exclusively by the observable attributes of people and places and conditionally independent once such attributes are controlled for. We address this tension by capturing the effect of relational structures through the interdependence traces they leave in aggregate data, using a recently proposed statistical network model. Comparing degree student mobility with Erasmus exchanges across 29 European countries—two cases involving similar populations but distinct institutional architectures—we show that relational structures shape destination choices in ways that differ systematically across institutional contexts and that standard models cannot capture. Accounting for interdependence also alters conclusions about conventional predictors, including geographic distance. Modelling relational structure is thus not a technical refinement but a necessary step toward aligning empirical migration research with its theoretical foundations.

articles.title: A bibliometric overview of Mauro Boianovsky’s legacy
articles.abstract: This paper offers a bibliometric overview of the scholarly legacy of Mauro Boianovsky. Drawing on data from Scopus and cross-referenced with his Currículo Lattes, we analyze a corpus of 100 works published between 1987 and 2024 and identify patterns in his publication outlets, thematic evolution, and intellectual networks. The results highlight his strong engagement with leading history of economics journals and reveal two core clusters structuring his scholarship: the history of macroeconomics cluster (with special emphasis on Knut Wicksell) and the history of development economics cluster (with contributions on Evsey Domar, Celso Furtado, and Latin American structuralism). The analysis also uncovers the integrative role of growth economics in bridging these agendas. Citation data confirms the enduring influence of Boianovsky’s work on secular stagnation, liquidity trap, development theory, and structuralism. Beyond reaffirming well-known aspects of his research, this study provides a quantitative mapping that situates his oeuvre within broader intellectual trajectories.

articles.title: Diversity and Structural Change in International Migration, 1960–2020
articles.authors: Micol Matilde Morellini, Per Block, Guy Abel
articles.abstract: Whether international migration has become more diverse in recent decades is a central question in the migration globalisation and integration literature, and one that different studies have answered inconsistently. We argue that these inconsistencies are not merely the result of different measurement or data choices, but a substantive finding: existing diversity indices capture different parts of the distribution of flows across origin–destination corridors, and those parts have moved in opposite directions over time. Using Hill profiles, which nest different diversity indices as special cases of a single continuous function, and new bilateral flow estimates for 195 countries from 1960 to 2020, we identify two distinct eras of global migration diversity: expanding connectivity through the 1980s, followed by growing evenness from the 1990s onwards. A counterfactual decomposition shows that these eras reflect separate processes: corridor expansion in earlier periods, and reallocation of migration mass across persistent corridors in more recent ones. Moving beyond global aggregates, we show that country-level inflow and outflow diversity followed highly heterogeneous trajectories that align with country-specific events and policy regimes. Migration globalisation is therefore best understood not as a uniform process, but as a set of uneven distributional changes operating differently across countries and time.

articles.title: LAND, SPACE OR CITIES: A HISTORY OF ‘URBAN ECONOMICS’ AS A FIELD
articles.authors: JHET Assistant, Beatrice Cherrier, Anthony Rebours
articles.abstract: The field of ‘Urban Economics’ is an elusive object, whose US-based origins, development, and internationalization we attempt to document in this paper. To flesh out urban economists’ territory, we rely on a mix of quantitative analysis (networks of authors most cited alongside the foundational contributions of Alonso, Muth and Mill) and archival research. We identify several periods in the development of American urban economics, including a taking-off in the 1960s, fueled both by scholarly contributions, urban riots and foundations’ grants, a marginalization in the 1980s, and a recent renewal where urban economists grappled with the theoretical legacy of the ‘New Economic Geography,’ and with the transfer of new empirical techniques from neighboring fields.

articles.title: Book Review of Economic Theory in the Twentieth Century: An Intellectual History. Volume III: 1946–Mid-1970s by Roberto Marchionatti
articles.abstract: Roberto Marchionatti’s third book in his four-volume history of twentieth-century economic theory covers the period from the end of the Second World War to the mid-1970s and explores the theoretical consolidation of what is often called the Neoclassical-Keynesian synthesis as well as the consolidation of neoclassical economics during the post-war era.

articles.title: Book Review of The Eye of the Master: A Social History of Artificial Intelligence by Matteo Pasquinelli
articles.abstract: The thesis of this history of artificial intelligence (AI) can be summed up in two propositions. AI is not a new development but has roots extending back at least to the eighteenth century; and developments in AI echo the structures of the societies in which they occurred. Although it draws heavily on theories developed by historians of science (the book serves as a reminder that, although economists are often criticized for being too theoretical, many historians are just as committed to theorizing), its main theme comes from Marx, whose ideas are extensively discussed. Pasquinelli argued that it was Marx who questioned whether it was technological developments embodied in machinery that determined the division of labour or the other way round. Pasquinelli substitutes AI for the machinery with which Marx was concerned.

articles.title: Mauro Boianovsky on Samuelsonian dynamics and the economic analysis of market processes
articles.abstract: In his article “Paul Samuelson’s ways to macroeconomic dynamics” Mauro Boianovsky has provided an account of the evolution of Samuelson’s attempts to construct a dynamic theory that, because of Samuelson’s centrality to modern economics, verges on being an account of the history of recent thought on the subject. This paper argues that Samuelson’s views should be related not only to the formal dynamic modeling of Frisch and Tinbergen, but also to the verbal accounts of dynamics and market processes found in work by Marshall, J. M. Clark, Chamberlin and Schumpeter that he had studied very carefully. Broadening our perspective in this way helps make sense of some otherwise puzzling features of Samuelson’s economics.

articles.title: Care for dissonant heritage from within and outside: volunteers and abandoned cemeteries in the Sudetenland
articles.abstract: In the years following the Second World War, German cemeteries and churchyards in the Sudetenland were vandalised, plundered and abandoned. Czech local authorities have largely lacked the will or resources to maintain them, despite bilateral obligations, and the sites remain uncomfortable evidence of a past that unsettles national narratives. This paper examines a ‘heritage from below’ response: volunteers who clear, restore and revitalise these dissonant burial grounds. Drawing on ethnographic fieldwork in cemeteries in the Ústí nad Labem Region (2025–2026) that included interviews with 15 volunteers from seven initiatives caring for nine cemeteries, the paper explores why people choose to care for heritage that local communities associate with guilt, anger and resentment. Volunteers’ aims developed organically from ‘rescue’ towards creating places of remembrance and contemplation. Volunteer labour was sustained by sociability, the satisfaction of physical work, respect for the dead and, among leaders, a sense of reparation and reconciliation. Engaging critically with the concept of ‘heritage from within’, which presumes a biographical attachment to the heritage cared for, the paper argues that the volunteers’ status as outsiders was central to their capacity to engage with, and at times set aside, the dissonance of these sites.

articles.title: Book Review of A History of Economic Thought in France by Gilbert Faccarello and Claire Silvant (eds.)
articles.abstract: A History of Economic Thought in France, edited by Gilbert Faccarello and Claire Silvant, is a two-volume work that brings together a distinguished group of scholars with long-standing expertise in French political economy. The first volume, Political Economy in the Age of Enlightenment, comprises nine chapters and covers the development of economic thought in France from the late 17th century to the eve of the French Revolution. The second volume, The Long Nineteenth Century, continues the narrative across the 19th century, tracing the transformation of economic reasoning amid liberal, formalist, and critical traditions. These volumes offer fresh insights and demonstrate the originality of French contributions to political economy, often neglected or underestimated in Anglophone scholarship. Together, the volumes situate economic ideas within their broader intellectual, political, and cultural contexts.

articles.title: Mauro Boianovsky: An Exemplary Scholar
articles.authors: JHET Assistant, FELIPE ALMEIDA, John Berdell
articles.abstract: This study introduces the late Mauro Boianovsky (1959–2024), one of the most distinguished historians of economics of his generation. Drawing on interviews and correspondence with his colleagues, co-authors, former students, and his sister, the study offers a portrait of his academic trajectory and intellectual contributions. It examines Boianovsky’s connection to Brasília and the University of Brasília (UnB), his training as an economist/historian of economics, and his engagement with colleagues and the broader history of economics community. The study aims to provide a lasting record of a remarkable scholar and to make the significance of Boianovsky’s contributions accessible to future generations. As the introduction to this symposium, it also briefly presents the other papers included in the collection.

articles.title: Book Review of Relocating Development Economics: The First Generation of Modern Indian Economists by Maria Bach
articles.abstract: The product of PhD research at King’s College London, this fine volume discusses the work of the first generation of Indian economists between the last quarter of the nineteenth century and the early twentieth century. Maria Bach’s original question, in her own terms, was to explore “how the first generation of modern Indian economists functioned in a Eurocentric world on their own terms and in what ways they challenged the status quo” (p. 157). Those Early Nationalists, as they came to be collectively known, built on ideas they had absorbed as students in the British imperial university system, to create “original, forward-thinking knowledge on economic development” (p. 3).

articles.title: Book Review of "Otto Neurath in Britain" by Christopher Burke and Ádám Tamás
articles.abstract: Otto Neurath praised the merits of war economy from 1909 and argued for using his visual method in peace propaganda in 1933. He worked as the director of the Soviet IZOSTAT in the early 1930s and developed anti-Soviet visual propaganda for the British Ministry of Information from the late 1930s. He advocated the highbrow philosophy of logical empiricism in Vienna, and built a ground-to-earth, comprehensible anti-culture of visual facts called "Isotype" in London. Based on this, one might think that Neurath was changing sides and world views too frequently, which would, no doubt, make it harder to perceive him as a likeable character. But this is not necessarily the case. This impressive new book, Otto Neurath in Britain, portrays the minutiae of the misadventures of Neurath, and, by doing so, unpacks the apparent contradictions in his many-sided and quite controversial legacy.

articles.title: The “Official opponent”? Wassily Leontief’s Idea of Econometric Methods, and the “Expansion of the Field of Direct Observation”
articles.abstract: Several recent works have explored Wassily Leontief’s distinction between standard econometrics, which he called “indirect statistical inference,” and a “direct induction” he called “direct observation.” These works usually understand Leontief’s direct induction through the lens of input-output analysis. I argue that this is too narrow a perspective. Instead, I show how this distinction stemmed from Leontief’s (1929, 1932a) econometric work, when he developed a statistical technique for determining supply and demand curves. By examining lesser-known published texts by Leontief from this period, as well as unpublished material from the archives, it appears that Leontief’s distinction was in part borrowed from Marschak (1931) when they were both in Germany. Like Marschak, Leontief distinguished between two epistemic strategies: indirect, using data from the marketplace, i.e., price-quantity data; or direct, using specific data separately on buyers (e.g., household surveys) and on sellers (e.g., plant surveys). This result fundamentally revises our understanding of Leontief's view of econometrics.

articles.title: Quantitative, Qualitative, or Mixed Methods: Explicitness, Prevalence, and Interrelationship of Methodological Orientations. An empirical study of sociological research using contextual language modelling and bibliometric analyses
articles.abstract: We apply scientometric techniques and methods of automated content analysis to the question of the quantitative, qualitative, and mixed-methods orientations prevalent in published sociological research. We consider the methodological orientation of the articles as well as corresponding journal characteristics. In terms of scholarly reception, we examine patterns of mutual citation. Our empirical analyses are based on data from the Web of Science Core Collection/Social Science Citation Index. At the same time, we provide a concise introduction to some of the basic procedures of relevant computational techniques. We are particularly interested in productive links between conventional scientometric techniques and recently developed language models.

articles.title: Grandchild care, paid work, and cognitive functioning in later life: Heterogeneity across gender and education among grandparents in Europe
articles.authors: Maria Karlene Shawn Cabaraban, Valeria Bordone, Daniela Weber, Bruno Arpino
articles.abstract: As working lives increasingly overlap with grandparenthood, grandparents may increasingly take on childcare responsibilities alongside paid work. By keeping grandparents mentally and socially engaged, this dual engagement may be cognitively enriching but unequal caregiving demands and educational stratification across gender likely differently shape opportunities and constraints. Drawing on role enhancement and role strain theories, we investigate whether the association between grandchild care provision and cognitive functioning differs between working and retired grandparents, once accounting for gender and education. Using a longitudinal sample of 18,748 grandfathers (N = 69,194) and 22,642 grandmothers (N = 79,702) aged 50-80 from the Survey of Health, Ageing, and Retirement in Europe (SHARE), we estimate cross-lagged panel models with individual fixed-effects (CLPM-FE) to examine contemporaneous and lagged associations of grandchild care provision and frequency with cognitive functioning (memory recall and verbal fluency), while mitigating concerns about reverse causality and time-invariant unobserved heterogeneity. Results show that, generally, grandchild care is positively associated with cognitive functioning for both genders but only during retirement and particularly for the higher-educated grandparents. Among working grandmothers, however, findings reveal a more nuanced picture: monthly or less frequent childcare is contemporaneously associated with improved verbal fluency, whereas childcare at both frequencies shows a negative lagged associated with memory recall. Together, these results highlight how the cognitive implications of childcare depend on other responsibilities that grandparents hold and point to the need for policies that support the reconciliation of paid work and family care in later life as these domains increasingly overlap.

articles.title: Foundational Asymmetry and the Federal Consolidation Problem: Somalia in Comparative Perspective
articles.abstract: Federal theory usually assumes that a center exists before the units it decentralizes to, or that sovereign units create a center together at one founding moment. A growing number of post-conflict federations follow neither path: member states are built first, and a central government is rebuilt later and then seeks authority over them. This article theorizes these latecomer-center federations. It argues that their stability depends less on how much authority the center holds than on whether central authority grows through shared-rule institutions. Three concepts specify the argument. Centralization without federal consolidation is the expansion of effective central authority before the procedures that define and constrain it are settled. Foundational asymmetry is the unequal institutional inheritance that units bring into a formally symmetric federation. Constituent compact consciousness is a unit's historically grounded claim to have co-authored the compact and therefore to take part in revising it. From these concepts the article derives four general propositions and a typology that places latecomer-center federations alongside coming-together and holding-together federations. It traces the mechanism in Somalia (1998–2025), where Puntland predates the federal government by fourteen years and the Provisional Constitution itself encodes its prior status, and then compares four latecomer-center federations: Iraqi Kurdistan, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Sudan before 2011 and Ethiopia. The comparison yields a second finding. Resistance takes a different form at each level of inherited capacity: units with materially established institutions withhold recognition and threaten exit, while units whose capacity rests on a founding claim and on recognition by the center escalate to violence when recognition is withdrawn. The framework explains why formally identical centralizing measures provoke unequal resistance, why procedural disputes escalate into disputes over the federation's authority, and why building a strong center and building a federation are distinct tasks. The comparison also shows that the form resistance takes depends on what the older unit holds: institutions it can withhold, a territory it can leave, or an army it can use.

articles.title: Trinity or Trilemma? How researchers assess publications, data and software
articles.authors: Judith Hartstein, Nathalie Schwichtenberg, Alexander Schniedermann
articles.abstract: Understanding what encourages researchers to (re)use publications, data and software and thereby trusting the output of distant and unknown peers, is essential for envisioning future forms of scholarly communication and developing organizational and technical infrastructures. With a survey among more than 1,700 researchers across disciplines we investigate a) how often researchers across the spectrum of disciplines use the three types of resources, and b) how they make the respective use decisions along ten assessment vectors. We find that resource use and assessment practices stabilize across disciplines in line with the integration of a resource into scientific practice, and that assessment practices fall into the three categories of resource specificity, field specificity and user specificity. We contextualize our findings within the broader discourse on epistemic trust, and we conclude that publications, data and software are always to be considered in reference to their similarities, synergies and diversities when it comes to scientific best practices and infrastructure development.

articles.title: ENVIRONMENT AND DEVELOPMENT IN EARLY TWENTIETH-CENTURY BRAZIL: FRANCISCO SIMCH’S POLITICAL ECONOMY OF COAL
articles.abstract: Influenced by nineteenth-century German economists, the Brazilian mining engineer, lawyer, and professor of political economy Francisco R. Simch (1877–1937) combined economic theory and policy to argue for the exploration of coal mines in Southern Brazil. His interdisciplinary treatment of the issue aligned environmental conservation and regional development, calling for an investigation into his work as representative of an approach to the interlinkages between environment and development belonging to the history of natural resource and environmental economics. He discussed the regulatory role of government, the importance of railways, the need to create industry-specific quality standards for “national coal” to compete internationally, and benefits in terms of balance of payments as well as of the protection of forests against the industrial use of firewood. The article unveils Simch’s political economy as a set of integrated arguments in favor of a transition into coal as an essential source of energy to the belated but steady drive for industrialization in the country.

articles.title: Peer Review and the Technical Soundness of Research: Evidence from Automated Audits of Political Science Working Papers
articles.abstract: Peer review is meant to select high quality work and make it better. To measure one dimension of quality (“technical soundness”), we develop method-specific checklists and a “universal checklist” derived from the published literature by a transparent, rule-based procedure. We then have a language-model coder apply these checklists to 798 working papers posted from 2020 to 2022 on three preprint servers and to 406 corresponding published versions. A one standard deviation increase in preprint soundness is associated with a 10.3 percentage point increase in publication probability and higher journal placement. For the published/unpublished margin, both the universal and the method-specific checklists predict publication outcomes to a similar degree. A “naive” review by the same model, with no checklist, predicts publication about as well overall and less well for top-three journals, but the checklists catch issues this misses and add further predictive power. Published versions score modestly higher than preprints: 67% score higher at publication, and the mean overall score rises by +0.19 standard deviations. We release the checklists and the auditing system as a tool for authors.

articles.title: Leveraging AmCAT to Validate Democracy Research
articles.authors: Soﬁa Gil-Clavel, Wouter van Atteveldt, Jana Bernhard-Harrer, Johannes B. Gruber, Kasper Welbers, Hajo G. Boomgaarden, Mariken van der Velden
articles.abstract: Validation of text and multimedia data remains a central concern for measurement quality in political and democracy studies. Validation should entail the reporting of performance metrics and the systematic construction of a credible chain of evidence supporting a measurement claim. As validation is more than merely contrasting human and machine annotations, validation must be accompanied by enough evidence, data provenance, documentation, and computational materials for an independent researcher to understand what was validated, against what, under which conditions, and with what limitations. Yet implementing these practices requires considerable time and effort, a burden that currently falls largely on individual researchers. It is here where MEDem AmCAT can help. In this article, we introduce MEDem AmCAT and show how it provides the infrastructure where political and democracy researchers can perform the full validation cycle: measurement assessment, data and provenance documentation, workflow reproducibility, and workflow assessment.

articles.title: Cold Homes, Colder Trust: Does Wartime Infrastructure Deprivation Erode Social Capital?
articles.authors: Ruslana Moskotina, Danyil Karakai, Valentyn Hatsko, Dmytro Andreiev, Kateryna Antonets​
articles.abstract: How does infrastructural deprivation as a form of wartime victimisation relate to civilians’ social capital? Drawing on two-wave panel data from Kyiv residents in winter 2025-2026, amid intensified Russian strikes on energy infrastructure, we examine whether deprivation erodes trust and prosociality through the negative affect it generates. We find deprivation associated with lower interpersonal and political trust via negative affect. For political trust, a direct association also emerges, though not across all specifications. Prosociality, by contrast, relates to deprivation only directly, suggesting a resource-based rather than affective mechanism. The associations are modest, indicating notable resilience of Kyiv’s social fabric.

articles.title: Commerce and Peace in the French Revolution: Rougier-Labergerie’s International Political Economy
articles.abstract: This study examines the political economy of international trade and perpetual peace proposed by the agronomist Jean-Baptiste Rougier-Labergerie under the French Directory. Drawing on Rougier-Labergerie’s treatise on commerce and peace, this article shows how a political economy that was rooted in natural jurisprudence navigated the challenges of subsistence and war through turbulent times that extended beyond the Thermidor. Similar to eighteenth-century intellectuals who witnessed large-scale wars waged with public debt in the name of national interest, Rougier-Labergerie considered the possibility of peace and prosperity to be intricately linked to the question of commercial rivalry between nations. He thereby recognized the pressing need to mitigate—by different means from those deployed by the radicals of Year II—the jealousy of trade that plagued Europe in the 1790s. This examination provides a more nuanced dimension to the established categories in historical inquiries into the international political economy of the revolutionary period.

articles.title: Adam Smith on the “wretched spirit of monopoly” in the East Indies trade
articles.abstract: According to Adam Smith, the “wretched spirit of monopoly” dogged the East Indies trade. The regulations that governed the East Indies trade established legal barriers or restrictions to entry and sustained a mercantile community whose interests were “the opposite to that of the great body of the people”. The East Indies charter conferred a special privilege that shielded the English East India Company from all domestic competition in Asian trade. The East India Company was the complete incarnation of a mercantile system against which Smith had determined to launch “a very violent attack” in Wealth of Nations (Smith 1987, p. 251). Smith’s mistrust of trading bodies like the East India Company was compounded by its having assumed political powers commensurate with the sovereign while still in possession of its monopolistic franchise. Smith’s proposal was, first, to abolish the monopolistic franchise to rid society of “the unfortunate effects of all the regulations of the mercantile system”, and second, reform the East India Company’s administrative duties and functions in the Indian territories. The contention of this paper is that Smith’s call to abolish the East Indies monopoly was inseparable from his appeal for reform of the English East India Company.

articles.title: Housing-welfare trade-off and young people's homeownership

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: States were instrumental in driving a homeownership boom in the second half of the 20th century. Yet, scholars have long been startled by an empirical fact that countries with more generous welfare states tend to have lower rates of homeownership. Building on this, various theories have attempted to explain a trade-off between welfare state and homeownership, often with the assumption that countries can either have stronger welfare states or higher homeownership levels. In this paper, using data from EU-SILC 2008-2019 for 21 European countries, we show that this seemingly negative association is mainly due to neglecting the housing status of young people. Most young people living with their parents may live in owner-occupied homes, but they do not formally own a house. And accounting for this fact and measuring homeownership at the individual level virtually eliminates the negative association between welfare state generosity and homeownership. This is mostly because living in parental home is more common among young people in countries with less generous welfare states and with high levels of owner-occupied homes such as Eastern or Southern Europe. Moreover, we also show based on multi-level models that more generous welfare state, in the form of higher minimum income schemes, social insurance and childcare provision, is associated with higher level of independent living among young people, and with higher individual homeownership among the higher earning group. Our findings challenge big trade-off theories and show that welfare states can support homeownership, specifically of young people.

articles.title: Zoning for Votes: How Local Politicians Use Land-Use Regulations for Political Gain
articles.abstract: Across many levels of governments, elected officials engage in opportunistic behavior, through political budget cycles or ‘pork-barrel’ spending. Local politicians, however, have more limited ability to manipulate spending or pass popular policies due to federalist budget constraints and preemption. In the face of these constraints, I argue that local politicians use the tools at their disposal, particularly land-use regulations, treating zoning as pork. Using both lot-level zoning data in New York City and national data on historic districts, I show that land-use changes occur disproportionately on municipal election years. This effect is driven by those with the strongest electoral incentives: politicians up for reelection in competitive districts. Additionally, this zoning political budget cycle is larger for density-restrictions, consistent with anti-density public opinion, and tends to target lots with politically active residents. These findings suggest strategic electoral incentives help explain why many cities have restricted new housing despite an affordability crisis.

articles.title: 500+ Job Applications Later: Reflections on the Economics PhD Job Market
articles.abstract: The economics PhD job market is a highly structured and centralized matching process that aims to reduce search frictions, yet remains intensely competitive, uncertain, and emotionally demanding for candidates. While much of what is known about candidates' experiences comes from personal anecdotes and informal conversations, this paper offers a first-person account of the 2025\textendash 2026 economics PhD job market, supported by descriptive empirical evidence from more than 500 applications across sectors, geographic regions, and institution types. Drawing on my experience as a candidate from a mid-ranked doctoral program, I document application patterns, first-round interview outcomes, and the practical and emotional challenges of navigating the recruitment process. Particular attention is given to less visible aspects of the market, including prolonged uncertainty and silence, limited communication from prospective employers, and the administrative burden of navigating different application systems. Rather than attempting to draw generalizable conclusions from a single candidate's experience, I offer a candid account of the measurable outcomes and personal difficulties of an extended job search. I hope this account provides future candidates with a more realistic understanding of what to expect and reassurance that rejection, uncertainty, and setbacks are common and do not necessarily reflect their abilities or research potential.

articles.title: Better land measures, same output report: GPS area, self-reported production and the inverse size–productivity relationship in Honduran coffee
articles.authors: Carlos de los Rios, José Antonio Mendoza Sánchez, Elena Serfilippi
articles.abstract: We compare the self-reported area of a coffee plot with its area measured by a high-accuracy GPS receiver for 1,443 producers in Honduras, and ask how the land measure affects the inverse size–productivity relationship. Among the 421 producers with a single plot, whose production and area refer to the same land, production rises one-for-one with the declared area (elasticity 0.993) and less than proportionally with the GPS area (0.620). With both measures in the same equation, the GPS coefficient is 0.001 (standard error 0.068): given the declared area, the GPS area adds no detectable information about reported production. This is what correlated errors in self-reported production and self-reported area produce. A better land measure does not give a cleaner test while production remains self-reported.

articles.title: Nocturnal Wayfaring: Walking in the dark
articles.authors: Hannah Dalgleish, Isabel M J Sargent

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: How do we find our way in the night? Cities after dark are brighter than ever before, changing how we experience, perceive, and navigate urban spaces at night. Our research asks: how can we come to know the night and our place in it? Through the metaphor of nocturnal wayfaring, we reflect on walking after dark in different nightscapes, alone or together, and from rural to urban environments. We draw upon our own night walks in the port city of Southampton in the South of England, first a reflexive nightnographic walk, and then, a transdisciplinary night walk with local experts. We propose that walking in the dark can be an act of cultivating care and bringing healing to the nighttime city. This work portrays a snapshot in time of a continuously evolving attempt to negotiate the complex narratives and liminal qualities of conducting nocturnal and transdisciplinary research in situ.

articles.title: Digital health interventions in public libraries: a JBI scoping review
articles.authors: Xavier Chan, Tracey Hartness, Rebekkah Curran, Paul Flowers, Megan Crawford
articles.abstract: Background: Digital health interventions offer opportunities to improve healthcare access but may exacerbate existing inequalities through the digital divide. Public libraries provide free access to digital technologies and are embedded within communities, positioning them as potential settings to support equitable access to digital health services. However, their role in facilitating digital health interventions remains under-explored. Objective: To map the existing evidence on digital health interventions delivered or facilitated within public library settings across geographical contexts. Methods: A scoping review was conducted in accordance with Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and reported using the PRISMA-ScR guidelines. Eligible sources included primary research and relevant grey literature published between 2002 and 2025, involving adults and adolescents in public library settings. Evidence was charted and synthesised using descriptive frequency analysis and narrative synthesis. Results: Twelve studies published between 2016 and 2024 were included. Eleven studies were conducted in the United States and one in the United Kingdom. Four categories of digital health interventions were identified: telemedicine (n=6), virtual reality (n=3), digital therapeutics (n=2) and online health education (n=1). Findings highlighted the potential of public libraries to improve access to healthcare, particularly for rural communities and digitally excluded populations. Free access to technology, staff support and trusted community environments facilitated engagement. However, implementation challenges included limited resources, staff capacity, privacy and confidentiality concerns, and mental health stigma. Conclusion: Public libraries represent a promising but underdeveloped setting for facilitating equitable access to digital health interventions. Further research across diverse geographical contexts and intervention types is needed to understand implementation requirements and inform sustainable service development.

articles.title: ‘Neutral’ Ground or Party Ground? Right-Wing Populism and the Subnational Politics of Adult Education in Germany
articles.authors: Renan Sari Winkler, Hung H. V. Nguyen
articles.abstract: As RWPPs become central political actors in local-level policymaking, the question arises if and how this development influences democracy building and integration. Adult education policy is crucial for these domains and is heavily influenced by local-level politics. We expect that RWPPs aim to reduce courses in the fields of civic education, environment, diversity, and integration. Germany is an ideal case to study this phenomenon, and we therefore investigate the impact of the AfD’s rhetorical and electoral strength at the local level on adult education course provision. We use data from the Local Manifesto Project, county-level seat shares, and adult education course provision (2009-2023). Applying an automated, sentiment-based text analysis of local manifestos and estimating within-county models, our findings do not reveal that RWPPs affect course provision in the respective areas systematically. This suggests that political ‘firewalls’ and the institutional resilience of adult education providers continue to restrict RWPPs influence.

articles.title: Saturation Prompting: Recovering Stable Categories from Open-Ended Survey Responses with Repeated LLM Extraction
articles.abstract: A single large language model (LLM) call cannot reliably find the categories in open-ended survey responses because the model samples from a probability distribution and returns different themes each run, so one list cannot tell which belong to the data and which to that draw. The pipeline documented here improves reliability and reproducibility through saturation prompting, in which many independent calls each read a fresh random sample. It counts how often each theme is found and gives a distribution rather than a flat list. For researchers who want a shorter list, the pipeline can also merge labels with the same meaning into a final scheme of distinct categories. To test the pipeline, I apply saturation prompting to four open-ended survey questions from the UC Berkeley Social Networks Study and compare the results with a single call to the same model. Against the study’s existing codebooks, built by hand and independently, Llama 3.1 8B saturation runs recover 43 to 47 of their 50 categories, against 31 to 37 for its single calls, with the gain on the two more interpretive questions; on the two concrete questions a single call already finds most of them. On a more capable model, Claude Sonnet 5, saturation prompting adds less than it does for Llama over a single prompt asking the model to extract as many categories as it can find. Still, for both models and on every question, saturation finds more distinct categories than a single call. Llama’s additions include whole broad categories, while Sonnet’s are mostly more nuanced distinctions within broad categories its single call already finds. Saturation prompting makes a lower-tier open-weight model that can run on a laptop more reproducible by reducing run-to-run variability. Averaged across the four questions, the similarity between two runs’ ten most frequent labels rises from 0.85 for a single call to 0.96 with 64 calls (1.0 = identical meaning). Merging, although convenient, keeps only 33 to 91 percent of the distinct categories a saturation run finds.

articles.title: State cooperation policies and local political geography explain spatial patterns in U.S. immigration enforcement, 2023-2026
articles.authors: Asad L. Asad, David Broska, Gerard Torrats-Espinosa
articles.abstract: Immigration enforcement, which includes arrests of noncitizens in law enforcement custody (``law enforcement arrests'') and those made in the community (``community arrests''), can occur in any U.S. county. Yet some counties experience more of one or both types of immigration enforcement than other counties, and these spatial patterns can vary across presidential administrations. We evaluate two theoretical explanations for these patterns: (1) state cooperation policies that require or circumscribe federal-local collaboration in immigration enforcement, and (2) political geography, whereby immigration enforcement aligns with the ostensible partisan interests of local voters. Drawing on immigration arrest data between December 3, 2023 and August 5, 2026, we examine the patterning of immigration arrests across counties in the second Trump administration relative to the Biden administration. We find that state cooperation policies and political geography both matter for where arrests occur, but they operate under distinct conditions. Relative to the Biden administration, immigration arrests during the Trump administration have increased in most counties, regardless of state cooperation policies. But immigration arrests, particularly law enforcement ones, have increased most where states require rather than limit cooperation. Law enforcement arrests have also increased most where President Trump won a larger share of votes in the 2024 election, regardless of state cooperation policies. By contrast, community arrests have increased most where state policies require federal-local cooperation in immigration enforcement and where President Trump won more votes. Surges in community arrests have been most likely where Vice President Harris received more votes than President Trump, regardless of state cooperation policies. We conclude that, alongside state cooperation policies, political geography may represent an undertheorized explanation for spatial differences in immigration enforcement across presidential administrations.

articles.title: Why We Should Stop Using the Term Gendered Family Violence
articles.abstract: I support ending the use of gendered family violence as the organising description of family violence. Gendered theories and population patterns can inform research and prevention. They cannot by themselves establish who used violence, who experienced it, or why it occurred in an individual family. This analysis examines how gendered framing operates through service eligibility, referral pathways and the ordering of competing inquiries. In Australia, the State of Victoria’s Orange Door and Multi-Agency Risk Assessment and Management (MARAM) materials document differences in service access and assessment pathways. Family Justice Council guidance in England and Wales gives domestic-abuse inquiries priority when considering allegations of alienating behaviour. These jurisdictions and arrangements differ: Victoria provides explicit gender-differentiated pathways; the Family Justice Council guidance prioritises domestic-abuse inquiries, whose relationship to gendered framing requires separate examination. The evidence examined raises questions about whether possible victimisation and perpetration receive equivalent scrutiny across genders. It does not establish the accuracy of every classification or reassessment. Transparent criteria and independent evaluation are needed. The analysis also questions whether the gendered framework adequately accounts for the available research, or gives supportive evidence greater standing than findings that challenge its organising assumptions. Research documents violence in more than one direction, including parental alienating behaviours affecting mothers and fathers. Assessment must examine conduct, context, effects and risk, while distinguishing protective responses from abusive conduct. Removing gendered from the organising description would leave gender-related explanations available wherever supported by evidence. Assessment standards, service pathways, and error correction must also be accountable to that evidence.

articles.title: Assessment Without a Waiting Clock: Language, Learning Needs and Institutional Responsibility for Newly Arrived Pupils in Nordic Schools
articles.abstract: When a newly arrived pupil struggles in the language of schooling, the difficulty may reflect limited opportunities to learn that language, an additional learning need, or both. Schools must act before those explanations can always be separated with confidence. This article examines that uncertainty as a problem of educational policy rather than simply a problem of test selection. Drawing on Nordic policy documents and research on multilingual assessment, inclusion and policy enactment, it argues against using time since arrival as a substitute for professional judgement. A distinction is proposed between three periods that are often blurred in administrative practice: residence in the receiving country, access to meaningful language instruction, and the interval between an identified concern and an educational response. The article develops a revisable assessment approach in which classroom support, evidence gathering and specialist evaluation can proceed together. It considers the consequences for family participation, local discretion, resources and administrative accountability. The proposed approach does not claim to identify disability through multilingual assessment alone, nor does it report original fieldwork. Its contribution is a policy argument: uncertainty about cause should not become uncertainty about whether a school must provide support.
